name: Arecaceae

lineage_context.teaching_goal: Teach the project palms through Sabal's costapalmate fan leaves, fibrous leaf sheaths, unarmed petioles, 3-part flowers and drupaceous fruits, then separate dwarf palmetto from Mexican palmetto by subterranean versus aerial trunk and weak versus strong costa.

project_scope.selection_mode: Sabal minor + Sabal mexicana project module
project_scope.note: Both species are accepted by current Kew and native-range treatments include Texas.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start with the leaf architecture. Project Sabal leaves are fanlike but not purely palmate: a central costa extends into the blade, producing a costapalmate fold pattern.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Perennial palms with solitary stems that may be subterranean or aerial. Leaves have fibrous sheaths, long unarmed petioles and broad fan blades divided into many induplicate segments.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Inflorescences arise among the leaves and branch into panicles. Flowers are small and fundamentally 3-merous, with 6 tepals and 6 stamens in Sabal.
family_diagnostics.fruit: One-seeded dark drupes/berrylike palm fruits on branched infructescences.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Costapalmate fan leaf + fibrous sheath + unarmed petiole + many small 3-part flowers = project Arecaceae/Sabal.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: fan leaf → costa/hastula → leaf sheath → inflorescence → fruit → S. minor vs S. mexicana → monocot comparison
visual_lesson.intro: Sabal palms are easiest to learn from leaf architecture first. The key is not just 'fan leaf'—it is a costapalmate fan with a real midrib-like costa extending into the blade.

steps.title: 1 · Find the costa inside the fan
steps.look_for: A central costa projects into the fan blade, creating a costapalmate rather than perfectly palmate leaf.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the defining Sabal leaf architecture.

steps.title: 2 · Find the hastula
steps.look_for: A triangular/rounded flap of tissue on the upper side where the petiole meets the blade.
steps.why_it_matters: Hastula shape is useful within Sabal and teaches a palm-specific structure.

steps.title: 3 · Compare trunk architecture
steps.look_for: Sabal minor usually has a subterranean stem with leaves appearing near ground level; S. mexicana develops a conspicuous aerial trunk.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the fastest project species split.

steps.title: 4 · Compare leaf strength and fibers
steps.look_for: S. minor weakly costapalmate, fewer leaves and generally no threadlike segment fibers; S. mexicana strongly costapalmate with filiferous segments.
steps.why_it_matters: Adds a second structural species check beyond trunk presence.

steps.title: 5 · Read the inflorescence
steps.look_for: Much-branched axillary inflorescence carrying many tiny 3-merous flowers.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirms the palm as an angiosperm rather than treating the crown only as foliage.

steps.title: 6 · Read the black fruits
steps.look_for: Dark round to oblate fruits; S. mexicana fruits are notably larger than those of S. minor.
steps.why_it_matters: Late-season confirmation and another species-level tie-breaker.

comparisons.title: Arecaceae vs Smilacaceae
comparisons.rule: Sabal is a self-supporting palm with large costapalmate leaves and branched flower/fruit panicles. Smilax is a climbing vine with tendrils, reticulate-veined leaves, umbels and berries.

comparisons.title: Sabal minor vs Sabal mexicana
comparisons.rule: S. minor = usually subterranean stem + weakly costapalmate leaves + inflorescence much longer than leaves + smaller fruit. S. mexicana = aerial trunk + strongly costapalmate filiferous leaves + larger fruit.

visual_lesson.caveat: Do not use height alone. Young S. mexicana can be short, and old S. minor can appear robust. Trunk position plus leaf costa/fibers and reproductive characters is safer.

genera.fast_cue: costapalmate fan leaf + fibrous sheath + unarmed petiole + small 3-merous flowers
